m-proof:
Key ideas
  • Proof by deduction: start from known facts and use logical steps to reach the statement in general.
  • Proof by exhaustion: split into a finite set of cases and check every one (e.g. n even / n odd, or n \equiv 0,1,2 \pmod 3).
  • Disproof by counter-example: a single case where the statement fails is enough.
  • Proof by contradiction: assume the statement is false, then show this leads to something impossible.
Useful forms
  • Even: 2k; odd: 2k+1; consecutive integers: n,\ n+1; rational: \frac{a}{b} with a,b \in \mathbb{Z}, b \neq 0, no common factors.
  • Completing the square proves positivity: x^2-6x+10=(x-3)^2+1>0 for all real x.
Classic proofs
  • **\sqrt{2} is irrational:** assume \sqrt2=\frac ab in lowest terms. Then a^2=2b^2, so a is even, a=2c, giving b^2=2c^2, so b is even too, contradicting "lowest terms".
  • Infinitely many primes: assume finitely many, p_1,\dots,p_n. Then N=p_1p_2\cdots p_n+1 leaves remainder 1 when divided by every p_i. So N is prime or has a prime factor not in the list. Contradiction.
Worked example

Prove that the sum of any three consecutive integers is divisible by 3.

n+(n+1)+(n+2)=3n+3=3(n+1)

3(n+1) is a multiple of 3, so the result holds for all integers n.

Exam tips

Write a concluding sentence that restates what has been proved, e.g. "…therefore it is divisible by 3".

  • In contradiction proofs, state clearly what you are assuming and where the contradiction is.
  • A list of examples is not a proof (unless it is exhaustion over *all* cases).
m-alg:
Indices and surds
  • a^m a^n=a^{m+n}, \ (a^m)^n=a^{mn}, \ a^{-n}=\frac1{a^n}, \ a^{\frac mn}=(\sqrt[n]a)^m.
  • Rationalise: \dfrac{1}{\sqrt a+\sqrt b}=\dfrac{\sqrt a-\sqrt b}{a-b}.
Quadratics
  • Discriminant b^2-4ac: >0 two real roots, =0 one repeated root, <0 no real roots.
  • Completed square a(x+p)^2+q gives the turning point (-p,\,q).
x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}
Inequalities
  • For a quadratic inequality, find the critical values and sketch. E.g. x^2-x-6<0 \Rightarrow -2<x<3.
  • Multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.
Polynomials
  • Factor theorem: f(a)=0 \iff (x-a) is a factor.
  • Algebraic division (or comparing coefficients) gives the other factor.
Functions
  • Composite fg(x)=f(g(x)): apply g first.
  • Inverse f^{-1}: swap x and y and rearrange. Its graph is the reflection of f in y=x. Domain of f^{-1} = range of f.
  • Modulus: solve |f(x)|=k using f(x)=\pm k, and check graphically.
  • Transformations: f(x)+a is up a; f(x+a) is left a; af(x) stretches vertically by factor a; f(ax) stretches horizontally by factor \frac1a.
Partial fractions
\frac{5x+1}{(x-1)(x+2)}=\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{x+2}

Put x=1: 6=3A, so A=2. Put x=-2: -9=-3B, so B=3.

  • For a repeated factor (x-a)^2 use \frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B}{(x-a)^2}.
Exam tips

For "show that" questions, every step must be visible. Don't jump straight to the given answer.

  • State the domain and range when asked about f^{-1}. Many marks are lost here.
m-coord:
Straight lines
  • Gradient m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}; line y-y_1=m(x-x_1).
  • Parallel lines have equal gradients. Perpendicular lines have m_1m_2=-1.
  • Midpoint \left(\frac{x_1+x_2}2,\frac{y_1+y_2}2\right); distance \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}.
Circles
(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2
  • Centre (a,b), radius r. Complete the square to convert x^2+y^2+2fx+2gy+c=0.
  • A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
  • A perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.
  • The angle in a semicircle is 90^\circ, so a right-angled triangle's hypotenuse is a diameter.
  • Line meets circle: substitute, then use the discriminant (>0 two points, =0 tangent, <0 none).
Parametric equations
  • x=f(t), y=g(t). To get the Cartesian form, eliminate t, e.g. using \sin^2t+\cos^2t=1.
  • Example: x=3\cos t, y=3\sin t gives x^2+y^2=9.
Worked example

Find the tangent to x^2+y^2-4x+6y-12=0 at (5,1).

Centre (2,-3), so the radius gradient is \frac{1-(-3)}{5-2}=\frac43. The tangent gradient is -\frac34:

y-1=-\tfrac34(x-5)\ \Rightarrow\ 3x+4y-19=0
Exam tips
  • Give the line in the form the question asks for (e.g. ax+by+c=0 with integers).
  • Watch your signs: in (x-a)^2 the centre is at +a.
m-seq:
Binomial expansion
(a+b)^n=\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom nr a^{n-r}b^r
  • For any rational n: (1+x)^n=1+nx+\frac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^2+\dots, valid for |x|<1.
  • For (a+bx)^n, first take out a^n: a^n\left(1+\frac bax\right)^n, valid for |x|<\left|\frac ab\right|.
Arithmetic sequences
u_n=a+(n-1)d
S_n=\tfrac n2\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]=\tfrac n2(a+l)
Geometric sequences
u_n=ar^{n-1}
S_n=\frac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}
S_\infty=\frac a{1-r}\ \ (|r|<1)
Other sequences
  • Recurrence u_{n+1}=f(u_n): increasing, decreasing or periodic (repeats with some order k).
  • Sigma notation: \sum_{r=1}^{n}1=n. Watch the start value.
Worked example

A geometric series has u_2=12 and S_\infty=64. Find r.

ar=12 and \frac a{1-r}=64, so 12=64r(1-r). This gives 16r^2-16r+3=0, i.e. (4r-1)(4r-3)=0, so r=\frac14 or r=\frac34.

Exam tips

Always state the validity range of a binomial expansion with a non-integer or negative n.

  • When solving S_n>k by logs, dividing by \ln r with r<1 flips the inequality.
m-trig:
Basics
  • Radians: \pi\text{ rad}=180^\circ. Arc length s=r\theta; sector area A=\frac12r^2\theta (\theta in radians).
  • Small angles: \sin\theta\approx\theta, \tan\theta\approx\theta, \cos\theta\approx1-\frac{\theta^2}2.
  • Sine rule \frac a{\sin A}=\frac b{\sin B} (watch for the ambiguous case). Cosine rule a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A. Area \frac12ab\sin C.
Identities
\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1
1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta
1+\cot^2\theta=\csc^2\theta
\sin(A\pm B)=\sin A\cos B\pm\cos A\sin B
\cos(A\pm B)=\cos A\cos B\mp\sin A\sin B
\sin2A=2\sin A\cos A
\cos2A=1-2\sin^2A=2\cos^2A-1
\tan2A=\frac{2\tan A}{1-\tan^2A}
Harmonic form

a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta=R\sin(\theta+\alpha), where R=\sqrt{a^2+b^2} and \tan\alpha=\frac ba.

  • Max value R, min value -R. Use it to solve equations and find extrema.
Inverse trig
  • \arcsin: domain [-1,1], range [-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2]. \arccos: range [0,\pi]. \arctan: range (-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2).
Worked example

Solve 2\cos^2x=1+\sin x for 0\le x<2\pi.

2(1-\sin^2x)=1+\sin x \Rightarrow 2\sin^2x+\sin x-1=0 \Rightarrow (2\sin x-1)(\sin x+1)=0.

So \sin x=\frac12, giving x=\frac\pi6,\frac{5\pi}6; or \sin x=-1, giving x=\frac{3\pi}2.

Exam tips

Check the interval and units (degrees or radians). Find all solutions using the CAST diagram or the graph's symmetry.

  • Never divide both sides by \sin x: you lose the solutions where \sin x=0. Factorise instead.
m-exp:
Key facts
  • y=a^x passes through (0,1). y=e^x has gradient equal to its value: \frac d{dx}e^{kx}=ke^{kx}.
  • \log_a x=n \iff a^n=x; \ln x=\log_e x.
\log a+\log b=\log ab
\log a-\log b=\log\tfrac ab
k\log a=\log a^k
  • Change of base: \log_a x=\frac{\ln x}{\ln a}.
Modelling
  • Growth/decay: N=N_0e^{kt} (k>0 growth, k<0 decay).
  • Linearising: if y=ax^n then \log y=\log a+n\log x (gradient n, intercept \log a). If y=kb^x then \log y=\log k+x\log b.
Worked example

Solve 3^{2x}-4\cdot3^x+3=0.

Let u=3^x: u^2-4u+3=0, so u=1 or u=3, giving x=0 or x=1.

Exam tips

In modelling questions, interpret the constants in context (e.g. N_0 is the initial value) and comment on limitations of the model.

  • \ln(a+b)\neq\ln a+\ln b. This is a very common error.
  • e^x>0 for all x, so reject any solution that needs e^x\le0.
m-diff:
Rules
\frac{d}{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1}
\frac{d}{dx}e^{kx}=ke^{kx}
\frac{d}{dx}\ln x=\frac1x
\frac{d}{dx}\sin kx=k\cos kx
\frac{d}{dx}\cos kx=-k\sin kx
\frac{d}{dx}\tan kx=k\sec^2kx
  • Chain rule: \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy}{du}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}. Product rule: (uv)'=u'v+uv'. Quotient rule: \left(\frac uv\right)'=\frac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}.
  • First principles: f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}.
Applications
  • Tangent gradient f'(a); normal gradient -\frac1{f'(a)}.
  • Stationary points where f'(x)=0: f''>0 minimum, f''<0 maximum.
  • Points of inflection: f''(x)=0 and f'' changes sign. Concave where f''<0, convex where f''>0.
  • Increasing where f'(x)>0.
Implicit and parametric
  • Implicit: differentiate each term w.r.t. x, so \frac d{dx}y^2=2y\frac{dy}{dx} and \frac d{dx}(xy)=y+x\frac{dy}{dx}.
  • Parametric: \frac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}.
  • Connected rates: \frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{dV}{dr}\cdot\frac{dr}{dt}.
Worked example

y=x^2e^{3x}: \ \frac{dy}{dx}=2xe^{3x}+3x^2e^{3x}=xe^{3x}(2+3x).

Exam tips

For the nature of a stationary point you must show the f'' value (or the sign change) and state the conclusion.

  • In optimisation, check that the answer makes sense (e.g. a length must be positive).
m-int:
Standard results
\int x^n\,dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+c\ (n\neq-1)
\int\frac1x\,dx=\ln|x|+c
\int e^{kx}dx=\tfrac1ke^{kx}+c
\int\cos kx\,dx=\tfrac1k\sin kx+c
\int\sin kx\,dx=-\tfrac1k\cos kx+c
  • \int\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}dx=\ln|f(x)|+c, and \int\sec^2kx\,dx=\frac1k\tan kx+c.
Techniques
  • Substitution: change dx and the limits.
  • By parts: \int u\frac{dv}{dx}dx=uv-\int v\frac{du}{dx}dx. Choose u to be the factor that simplifies when differentiated (but take u=\ln x).
  • Partial fractions for rational functions.
  • Trig identities, e.g. \cos^2x=\frac12(1+\cos2x).
Areas and differential equations
  • The area between curve and x-axis is \int_a^b y\,dx. Regions below the axis give negative values, so split them up.
  • Area between curves: \int(\text{top}-\text{bottom})\,dx.
  • Separable DE: \frac{dy}{dx}=f(x)g(y) \Rightarrow \int\frac1{g(y)}dy=\int f(x)\,dx. Use the initial conditions to find c.
  • Trapezium rule: \int_a^b y\,dx\approx\frac h2\left[y_0+2(y_1+\dots+y_{n-1})+y_n\right], where h=\frac{b-a}n.
Worked example

\displaystyle\int_1^e x\ln x\,dx: take u=\ln x, v'=x. Then

\left[\tfrac{x^2}2\ln x\right]_1^e-\int_1^e\tfrac x2\,dx=\tfrac{e^2}2-\tfrac{e^2-1}4=\tfrac{e^2+1}4
Exam tips

Don't forget +c on indefinite integrals, and the modulus in \ln|x|.

  • Trapezium rule: an overestimate if the curve is convex, an underestimate if concave.
m-num:
Locating roots
  • If f is continuous on [a,b] and f(a), f(b) have opposite signs, there is a root in (a,b).
  • It can fail if f has an asymptote in the interval, or if there are two roots close together.
Iteration
  • Rearrange f(x)=0 to x=g(x) and iterate x_{n+1}=g(x_n).
  • It converges if |g'(x)|<1 near the root. Staircase diagram if g'>0, cobweb if g'<0.
Newton–Raphson
x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}
  • It fails if f'(x_n)\approx0 (tangent nearly horizontal), or if the start value is far from the root.
Worked example

f(x)=x^3-2x-5, x_0=2: f(2)=-1 and f'(2)=10, so x_1=2.1.

To show a root is 2.09 to 2 d.p., check that f(2.085) and f(2.095) have opposite signs.

Exam tips

To justify accuracy, use the sign change on the bounds (\pm0.005 for 2 d.p.), then conclude in words.
m-vec:
Basics
  • \mathbf a=x\mathbf i+y\mathbf j+z\mathbf k; magnitude |\mathbf a|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}; unit vector \frac{\mathbf a}{|\mathbf a|}.
  • \overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other.
  • Position vector of a point dividing AB in the ratio m:n: \mathbf a+\frac m{m+n}(\mathbf b-\mathbf a).
  • Direction angle with the x-axis: \cos\theta_x=\frac x{|\mathbf a|}.
Geometry
  • Collinear points: show \overrightarrow{AB}=k\overrightarrow{BC} and that they share a point.
  • In 2D, a vector at bearing/angle \theta to \mathbf i with magnitude r is r\cos\theta\,\mathbf i+r\sin\theta\,\mathbf j.
Worked example

A(1,2,3) and B(4,6,3): \overrightarrow{AB}=3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j, so |AB|=5 and the unit vector is \frac15(3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j).

Exam tips

Show vector working clearly in column or \mathbf{ijk} form. In proofs, state the conclusion (e.g. "hence ABCD is a parallelogram").
s-samp:
Key terms
  • Population: the whole group. Census: observe every member. Sample: a subset.
  • Sampling frame: a list of the members of the population.
Methods
  • Simple random: every sample of size n is equally likely (random numbers or lottery).
  • Systematic: every k-th item from a list, with a random start; k=\frac Nn.
  • Stratified: sample from each stratum in proportion to its size, e.g. \frac{80}{200}\times30=12.
  • Quota: the interviewer fills quotas for each group. Non-random, so it may be biased, but no frame is needed.
  • Opportunity: whoever is available. Easy, but unlikely to be representative.
Large data set
  • Know the Edexcel LDS: weather data from UK and overseas stations, 1987 and 2015. "tr" means trace (under 0.05 mm of rain). Look out for n/a values.
Exam tips

When criticising a method, refer to the context (e.g. "only people at the gym at 9 am are sampled, so it is not representative").

  • Stratified and quota sampling both use groups. Stratified is random within each group; quota is not.
s-data:
Measures
\bar x=\frac{\sum x}n
\sigma^2=\frac{\sum x^2}n-\bar x^2=\frac{S_{xx}}n
  • Median and quartiles for grouped data come from interpolation. IQR =Q_3-Q_1.
  • Coding y=\frac{x-a}b: \bar y=\frac{\bar x-a}b and \sigma_y=\frac{\sigma_x}b.
Diagrams
  • Histogram: frequency density =\frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}; area is proportional to frequency.
  • Box plots: outliers are usually below Q_1-1.5\times\text{IQR} or above Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}.
  • Cumulative frequency: plot at the upper class boundaries.
Correlation and regression
  • PMCC r lies between -1 and 1. Correlation does not imply causation.
  • Regression line y=a+bx: interpret b as the change in y per unit of x. Only predict within the data range (interpolation).
Exam tips

When comparing distributions, compare a location (median or mean) and a spread (IQR or s.d.), both in context.

  • Use the median and IQR when there are outliers or skew.
s-prob:
Rules
P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)
  • Mutually exclusive: P(A\cap B)=0. Independent: P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B).
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}
  • Independence also means P(A\mid B)=P(A).
Tools
  • Venn diagrams: fill from the centre outwards.
  • Tree diagrams: multiply along branches and add between outcomes. The second-stage branches are conditional.
  • Two-way tables.
Worked example

P(A)=0.4, P(B)=0.5, P(A\cup B)=0.7. Then P(A\cap B)=0.2=0.4\times0.5, so A and B are independent.

P(A\mid B)=\frac{0.2}{0.5}=0.4.

Worked example 2 (tree diagram)

A bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are taken without replacement. Find P(\text{second red}\mid\text{first blue}) and P(\text{both same colour}).

  • P(R_2\mid B_1)=\frac34.
  • P(\text{same})=\frac35\cdot\frac24+\frac25\cdot\frac14=\frac{6}{20}+\frac{2}{20}=\frac25.
  • Without replacement, the second-stage probabilities change, so the events are not independent.
Exam tips

To prove independence, show a numerical equality such as P(A\cap B)=P(A)\times P(B) and state the conclusion.
s-dist:
Binomial X\sim B(n,p)
  • Conditions: fixed n; independent trials; two outcomes; constant p.
P(X=r)=\binom nr p^r(1-p)^{n-r}
  • Use cumulative tables or a calculator: P(X\ge r)=1-P(X\le r-1).
Normal X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)
  • Symmetric bell curve. About 68% of values lie within 1\sigma, 95% within 2\sigma, and 99.7% within 3\sigma. The points of inflection are at \mu\pm\sigma.
  • Standardise: Z=\frac{X-\mu}\sigma\sim N(0,1).
  • Normal approximation to B(n,p) when n is large and p\approx0.5: \mu=np, \sigma^2=np(1-p). Use a continuity correction, e.g. P(X\le 10)\to P(Y<10.5).
Worked example

X\sim N(50,4^2) with P(X>a)=0.1: \frac{a-50}{4}=1.2816, so a=55.1.

Worked example (binomial)

X\sim B(20,0.3). Then P(X=5)=\binom{20}{5}(0.3)^5(0.7)^{15}=0.179, and P(X\ge5)=1-P(X\le4)=1-0.238=0.762.

Common mistakes
  • Treating P(X<5) as P(X\le5) for a binomial: for discrete distributions, P(X<5)=P(X\le4).
  • Entering \sigma^2 into the calculator where it wants \sigma.
  • For a normal distribution P(X=a)=0, so < and \le give the same answer; for a binomial they do not.
Exam tips

Remember the variance is \sigma^2: N(50,16) means \sigma=4.

  • Discrete distribution: probabilities sum to 1.
s-hyp:
Method

1. State H_0 and H_1 in terms of the parameter (p, \mu or \rho).

2. Choose the significance level (e.g. 5%). For a two-tailed test, put 2.5\% in each tail.

3. Under H_0, find the probability of the observed value or more extreme (or find the critical region).

4. Compare, then conclude in context.

Binomial test
  • H_0: p=0.3, H_1: p>0.3. With X\sim B(20,0.3), test P(X\ge x_{\text{obs}}).
  • Critical region: the set of values that leads to rejecting H_0. The actual significance level is P(\text{in CR}\mid H_0).
Normal mean
\bar X\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}n\right)
Z=\frac{\bar x-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}
Correlation
  • H_0:\rho=0, H_1:\rho>0 (or <0, or \neq0). Compare r with the critical value from the table.
Exam tips

Write the conclusion with no certainty words: "There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level to suggest that the proportion has increased."
k-units:
SI units
  • Base units: m (length), kg (mass), s (time). Derived: N = kg m s⁻², J = N m, W = J s⁻¹.
  • Convert carefully: 1\text{ km h}^{-1}=\frac{1000}{3600}\text{ m s}^{-1}.
Modelling assumptions
  • Particle: mass at one point; ignore size and rotation.
  • Rod: rigid, has length but no thickness. Lamina: flat.
  • Light: massless. Inextensible: constant length, so connected objects have equal acceleration.
  • Smooth: no friction. Rough: friction acts.
  • g=9.8\text{ m s}^{-2} unless stated. Give answers to 2–3 s.f. when g=9.8 is used.
Exam tips

When a question asks you to "state an assumption", link it to the effect it has, e.g. "treat the ball as a particle, so air resistance is ignored".
k-kin:
Constant acceleration (suvat)
v=u+at
s=ut+\tfrac12at^2
s=\tfrac12(u+v)t
v^2=u^2+2as
s=vt-\tfrac12at^2
  • Vector form: \mathbf v=\mathbf u+\mathbf at, \mathbf r=\mathbf ut+\frac12\mathbf at^2.
Graphs
  • v–t graph: gradient is acceleration; area is displacement.
Variable acceleration
v=\frac{ds}{dt}
a=\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{d^2s}{dt^2}
s=\int v\,dt
v=\int a\,dt
Projectiles
  • Horizontal: u\cos\theta is constant. Vertical: u\sin\theta, with a=-g.
  • Time of flight (to the same level): \frac{2u\sin\theta}g. Max height: \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}.
Worked example

A ball is thrown at 20\text{ m s}^{-1} and 30^\circ above the horizontal. Vertical u_y=10, so it is at the top at t=\frac{10}{9.8}=1.02\text{ s}. The range on level ground is 20\cos30^\circ\times2.04=35.3\text{ m}.

Common mistakes
  • Using suvat when acceleration is not constant: use calculus instead.
  • Forgetting that g acts on the vertical motion only; horizontal velocity is constant in a projectile.
  • At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero, not the speed.
Exam tips

Choose and state a positive direction. Most suvat sign errors come from mixing directions.
k-force:
Newton's laws
  • N1: constant velocity unless a resultant force acts. N2: F=ma. N3: equal and opposite forces on different bodies.
  • Weight W=mg. On a slope at angle \alpha: mg\sin\alpha down the slope, mg\cos\alpha into the slope.
Friction
F\le\mu R
  • Limiting equilibrium or moving: F=\mu R. Friction opposes the motion (or the tendency to move).
Connected particles
  • Over a smooth pulley: same tension on both sides of a light string; same acceleration if the string is inextensible.
  • Write F=ma for each particle separately (or for the whole system if moving together).
Worked example

A 3 kg block on a rough horizontal table (\mu=0.2) is pulled by a string over a pulley to a hanging 2 kg mass.

For the 2 kg mass: 2g-T=2a. For the block: T-0.2(3g)=3a. Adding gives 2g-0.6g=5a, so a=2.74\text{ m s}^{-2} and T=14.1\text{ N}.

Exam tips

Draw a large force diagram for every body. Resolve parallel and perpendicular to the slope.
k-mom:
Moments
\text{moment}=F\times d_\perp
  • d_\perp is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. Unit: N m.
  • Equilibrium: resultant force =0 and total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment about any point.
  • Uniform rod: its weight acts at the centre.
  • "About to tilt" about a support: the reaction at the other support is 0.
  • Ladder problems: resolve vertically and horizontally, then take moments about the foot. Use F\le\mu R.
Worked example

A uniform 4 m plank of mass 20 kg rests on supports at end A and at B, 3 m from A. How far beyond B can a 50 kg person stand before the plank tips?

On the point of tipping about B, R_A=0. Taking moments about B: 20g\times1=50g\times d, so d=0.4\text{ m} beyond B (3.4 m from A).

Exam tips

Take moments about a point where an unknown force acts, which removes it from the equation.
p-1:
Planning and implementing
  • Independent variable: the one you change. Dependent variable: the one you measure. Control variables: kept constant.
  • Choose instruments with a suitable resolution, the smallest change they can show (e.g. a micrometer reads to 0.01 mm).
  • Repeat readings and take the mean, discarding anomalies. Check for zero errors.
Analysis
  • Accuracy: how close a value is to the true value. Precision: how close repeated readings are to each other.
  • Random errors cause scatter; reduce them by repeating and averaging. Systematic errors shift every reading the same way (e.g. a zero error); they are not reduced by repeating.
  • Straight-line graphs: compare with y=mx+c. Take the gradient from a large triangle.
  • Log graphs: if y=kx^n, then \lg y=n\lg x+\lg k, so the gradient is n.
Evaluation
  • Percentage difference from the accepted value: \frac{|\text{exp}-\text{accepted}|}{\text{accepted}}\times100\%.
  • Error bars show the uncertainty. Worst-fit lines give the uncertainty in the gradient.
Exam tips

"Suggest an improvement": be specific, e.g. "use a data-logger with a light gate to remove human reaction time", not just "be more accurate".
p-2-1:
SI base units
  • kg, m, s, A, K, mol (also cd). Every other unit is derived from these, e.g. N = kg m s⁻², J = kg m² s⁻², V = kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹, C = A s.
Prefixes
  • p 10^{-12}, n 10^{-9}, μ 10^{-6}, m 10^{-3}, c 10^{-2}, k 10^{3}, M 10^{6}, G 10^{9}, T 10^{12}.
Homogeneity
  • An equation is homogeneous if both sides have the same base units. This is necessary for the equation to be correct, but not sufficient (numerical constants such as \frac12 can't be checked this way).
Worked example

Check that E_k=\frac12mv^2 is homogeneous: \text{kg}\,(\text{m s}^{-1})^2=\text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-2}=\text{J} ✓.

Estimation
  • Mass of an adult ≈ 70 kg; walking speed ≈ 1.5 m s⁻¹; height of a room ≈ 2.5 m; power of a kettle ≈ 2 kW.
Exam tips

Convert everything to base SI units before substituting into equations. Squared prefixes trip people up: 1\text{ cm}^2=10^{-4}\text{ m}^2.
p-2-2:
Uncertainties
  • Absolute uncertainty: e.g. (2.40\pm0.05)\text{ m}. Percentage uncertainty =\frac{\Delta x}{x}\times100\%.
  • Adding or subtracting quantities: add the absolute uncertainties.
  • Multiplying or dividing: add the percentage uncertainties.
  • Powers: y=x^n gives (% in y) = n\times(% in x).
  • Uncertainty from repeat readings: \pm\frac12\timesrange.
  • From a graph: \%\text{ uncertainty}=\frac{|\text{best}-\text{worst gradient}|}{\text{best gradient}}\times100\%.
Worked example

Diameter d=(0.50\pm0.01) mm is a 2% uncertainty, so the area A=\frac{\pi d^2}{4} has uncertainty 2\times2\%=4\%.

Resistivity \rho=\frac{RA}{L} with R ±3% and L ±1%: the total is 3+4+1=8\%.

Significant figures
  • Give the final answer to the same number of s.f. as the least precise data.
  • The uncertainty in a mean is about half the range of the repeat readings. Anomalies are excluded before averaging.
Exam tips

Quote the final uncertainty to 1 (or 2) significant figures, and match the decimal places of the value to it.
p-2-3:
Scalars and vectors
  • Scalar: magnitude only (mass, speed, energy, distance). Vector: magnitude and direction (force, velocity, displacement, acceleration, momentum).
Combining vectors
  • Two perpendicular vectors: R=\sqrt{F_1^2+F_2^2}, at angle \theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{F_2}{F_1}.
  • Non-perpendicular: use a scale drawing, or the cosine rule (R^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C).
  • Equilibrium of three coplanar forces: they form a closed triangle.
Resolving
F_x=F\cos\theta,\qquad F_y=F\sin\theta
  • On a slope at \theta: the component of weight along the slope is mg\sin\theta; perpendicular to it is mg\cos\theta.
Worked example

A 12 N force acts at 30^\circ above the horizontal: F_x=12\cos30^\circ=10.4 N and F_y=6.0 N.

Exam tips

Make sure the angle you use is the one between the force and the direction you are resolving along.
p-3-1:
Definitions
  • Displacement s: distance in a given direction. Velocity v=\frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}. Acceleration a=\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}.
  • Graphs: the gradient of s–t is velocity; the gradient of v–t is acceleration; the area under v–t is displacement.
suvat (constant acceleration)
v=u+at
s=\tfrac12(u+v)t
s=ut+\tfrac12at^2
v^2=u^2+2as
Free fall and projectiles
  • Free fall: g=9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}. Measure g with light gates, a trapdoor and electromagnet, or video.
  • Projectiles: horizontal and vertical motion are independent. Horizontal velocity is constant (no air resistance); vertical acceleration is g.
  • Stopping distance = thinking distance (v\times reaction time) + braking distance.
Worked example

A ball is kicked horizontally at 8.0\text{ m s}^{-1} off a 20 m cliff. Vertically: 20=\frac12(9.81)t^2, so t=2.02 s. Horizontal distance: 8.0\times2.02=16 m.

Exam tips

List your s, u, v, a, t values first, and take one direction as positive (e.g. up = +, so a=-9.81).

  • Doubling the speed doubles the thinking distance but quadruples the braking distance.
p-3-2:
Forces
  • F=ma; weight W=mg. Drag increases with speed. Terminal velocity is reached when drag + upthrust = weight, so a=0.
  • Upthrust = weight of fluid displaced =\rho Vg (Archimedes).
  • Pressure p=\frac FA. In a fluid, p=h\rho g.
Moments and equilibrium
  • Moment =F\times d_\perp. Couple: torque =F\times perpendicular separation of the two forces.
  • Principle of moments: in equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments, and the resultant force is zero.
  • Centre of mass: the point where the weight appears to act.
Worked example

A 500 g object is fully submerged in water (\rho=1000\text{ kg m}^{-3}) with volume 2.0\times10^{-4}\text{ m}^3. Upthrust =1000\times2.0\times10^{-4}\times9.81=1.96 N, so its apparent weight is 4.91-1.96=2.95 N.

Exam tips

Free-body diagrams: label every force, and draw each arrow from the point where the force acts.
p-3-3:
Work done
W=Fx\cos\theta
  • Work done is the energy transferred when a force moves an object; it equals the force × the distance moved in the direction of the force.
  • 1 joule is the work done when a force of 1 N moves its point of application 1 m in the direction of the force.
  • A force at right angles to the motion (\theta=90^\circ) does no work, e.g. the normal reaction on a horizontal floor or a centripetal force.
  • The area under a force–displacement graph is the work done.
Kinetic and potential energy
E_k=\tfrac12mv^2,\qquad \Delta E_p=mg\Delta h
  • E_k=\frac12mv^2 comes from W=Fs with F=ma and v^2=2as.
  • mg\Delta h is valid near the Earth's surface, where g is constant.
Conservation of energy
  • Principle of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be transferred from one form to another. The total energy of a closed system is constant.
  • With no air resistance, a falling object's loss of E_p equals its gain in E_k: mgh=\frac12mv^2, so v=\sqrt{2gh} (independent of mass).
  • With resistive forces: loss of E_p = gain in E_k + work done against friction or drag.
Power and efficiency
P=\frac{W}{t}=Fv
\text{efficiency}=\frac{\text{useful output energy (or power)}}{\text{total input energy (or power)}}\times100\%
  • Power is the rate of doing work (rate of energy transfer); 1\text{ W}=1\text{ J s}^{-1}.
  • P=Fv follows from P=\frac{F\Delta x}{\Delta t}. At top speed, the driving force equals the resistive forces.
Worked examples

A car with a 30 kW engine has a top speed of 25\text{ m s}^{-1}. The resistive force is F=\frac Pv=\frac{30000}{25}=1200 N.

A 0.50 kg ball is dropped from 8.0 m and lands at 11\text{ m s}^{-1}. Loss of E_p=0.50\times9.81\times8.0=39.2 J; gain in E_k=\frac12\times0.50\times11^2=30.3 J. Work done against air resistance =39.2-30.3=9.0 J, so the average drag is \frac{9.0}{8.0}=1.1 N.

A motor lifts a 20 kg load through 3.0 m in 4.0 s, taking 250 W from the supply. Useful power =\frac{20\times9.81\times3.0}{4.0}=147 W, so the efficiency is \frac{147}{250}=59\%.

Common mistakes
  • Using the total distance instead of the distance along the force (use \cos\theta).
  • Using mass instead of weight in W=Fx (weight = mg).
  • Writing efficiency greater than 100%, or forgetting to square v in E_k.
Exam tips

In energy questions, write the energy statement in words first ("loss of GPE = gain in KE + work against drag"), then substitute. It earns method marks even if the arithmetic slips.
p-3-4:
Springs
  • Hooke's law: F=kx (up to the limit of proportionality).
  • Elastic potential energy E=\frac12Fx=\frac12kx^2, the area under the F–x graph.
  • Series springs: \frac1k=\frac1{k_1}+\frac1{k_2}. Parallel springs: k=k_1+k_2.
Materials
\sigma=\frac FA,\qquad \varepsilon=\frac xL,\qquad E=\frac\sigma\varepsilon
  • Young modulus unit: Pa. Find it from the gradient of the linear part of the stress–strain graph.
  • Elastic deformation: returns to its original shape. Plastic: permanent extension.
  • Ductile (copper): large plastic region. Brittle (glass): breaks with no plastic deformation. Polymeric (rubber): loading and unloading curves differ (hysteresis); the area between them is energy lost as heat.
  • UTS: the maximum stress a material can withstand.
Exam tips

Determining E for a wire: use a long wire (larger extension), measure the diameter with a micrometer in several places, and use the gradient of the stress–strain graph.
p-3-5:
Newton's laws
  • N1: a body stays at rest or at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts.
  • N2: F=\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}, which gives F=ma for constant mass.
  • N3: when A exerts a force on B, B exerts an equal and opposite force of the same type on A.
Momentum
p=mv,\qquad \text{impulse}=F\Delta t=\Delta p
  • Impulse is the area under the F–t graph (unit N s).
  • Momentum is conserved in a closed system.
  • Elastic collision: kinetic energy is also conserved. Inelastic collision: some kinetic energy is transferred to other forms.
Worked example

A 2.0 kg trolley at 3.0\text{ m s}^{-1} hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick together: 6.0=3.0v, so v=2.0\text{ m s}^{-1}. Kinetic energy goes from 9.0 J to 6.0 J, so the collision is inelastic.

Exam tips

Momentum is a vector, so give a sign to each direction. Airbags and crumple zones increase \Delta t, which reduces the force for the same \Delta p.
p-4-1:
Charge and current
I=\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}
  • 1 C is the charge passing a point when 1 A flows for 1 s. Elementary charge e=1.60\times10^{-19} C, so charge is quantised.
  • Kirchhoff's 1st law: the current into a junction equals the current out (conservation of charge).
  • In metals, the charge carriers are electrons. In electrolytes, they are ions.
Mean drift velocity
I=Anev
  • n is the number density of charge carriers. Metals have n\approx10^{28}\text{ m}^{-3}, so v is tiny (about mm s⁻¹). Semiconductors have a much smaller n.
Worked example

I=2.0 A in copper (n=8.5\times10^{28}) with A=1.0\times10^{-6}\text{ m}^2: v=\frac{2.0}{1.0\times10^{-6}\times8.5\times10^{28}\times1.6\times10^{-19}}=1.5\times10^{-4}\text{ m s}^{-1}.

Exam tips

If a wire narrows, the current is the same, so a smaller A means the drift velocity increases.
p-4-2:
Definitions
  • p.d. V=\frac WQ: energy transferred from electrical to other forms per unit charge. e.m.f. \varepsilon=\frac WQ: energy transferred to electrical form per unit charge.
  • Energy gained by an electron accelerated through V: eV=\frac12mv^2.
  • Resistance R=\frac VI. Ohm's law: I\propto V for a metallic conductor at constant temperature.
I–V characteristics
  • Resistor: a straight line through the origin. Filament lamp: a curve (resistance rises as it gets hotter). Diode: conducts only in forward bias, above about 0.6 V. LED: about 2 V.
  • NTC thermistor: resistance falls as temperature rises. LDR: resistance falls as light intensity rises.
Resistivity and power
R=\frac{\rho L}{A}
P=VI=I^2R=\frac{V^2}{R},\qquad W=VIt
  • 1 kWh =3.6\times10^6 J. Cost = kWh × price per kWh.
Exam tips

Resistivity is a property of the material; resistance depends on its dimensions too. For a metal, \rho rises with temperature.
p-4-3:
Circuit rules
  • Kirchhoff's 2nd law: around any loop, the sum of e.m.f.s equals the sum of p.d.s (conservation of energy).
  • Series: R=R_1+R_2+\dots Parallel: \frac1R=\frac1{R_1}+\frac1{R_2}+\dots
Internal resistance
\varepsilon=I(R+r),\qquad V=\varepsilon-Ir
  • "Lost volts" =Ir. A graph of V against I has gradient -r and y-intercept \varepsilon.
Potential divider
V_{out}=\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}V_{in}
  • With an LDR or thermistor in place of R_2, V_{out} responds to light or temperature (sensor circuits).
  • A potentiometer gives a continuously variable output.
Worked example

\varepsilon=6.0 V, r=0.50\ \Omega, R=5.5\ \Omega: I=\frac{6.0}{6.0}=1.0 A, so the terminal p.d. is V=5.5 V.

Exam tips

An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance; an ideal ammeter has zero resistance. In potential-divider questions, say what happens to R, then to V_{out}, and why.
p-4-4:
Wave basics
v=f\lambda,\qquad f=\frac1T
  • Progressive waves transfer energy. Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to the direction of travel; longitudinal waves oscillate parallel to it.
  • Phase difference =\frac{x}{\lambda}\times360^\circ. Intensity I=\frac PA, and I\propto A^2.
  • Only transverse waves can be polarised: their oscillations are restricted to one plane. Crossed polarising filters (or a metal grille for microwaves) block the wave.
Electromagnetic waves
  • All travel at c=3.00\times10^8\text{ m s}^{-1} in a vacuum. Order: radio, micro, IR, visible (400–700 nm), UV, X-ray, γ.
  • Refraction: n=\frac cv; n_1\sin\theta_1=n_2\sin\theta_2. Total internal reflection when \theta>C, where \sin C=\frac1n (going into air).
Superposition and stationary waves
  • Coherent sources: constant phase difference. Path difference n\lambda gives constructive interference; (n+\frac12)\lambda gives destructive.
  • Young's double slit: \lambda=\frac{ax}{D}. Grating: d\sin\theta=n\lambda.
  • Stationary waves form from two waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions. Node-to-node distance =\frac\lambda2. They store energy rather than transferring it.
  • Pipe closed at one end: L=\frac\lambda4 for the fundamental. String or open pipe: L=\frac\lambda2.
Exam tips

In Young's slits, a is the slit separation, x is the fringe spacing, and D is the slit-to-screen distance. Measure across several fringes and divide.
p-4-5:
Photons
E=hf=\frac{hc}{\lambda}
  • 1 eV =1.60\times10^{-19} J. LEDs can be used to find h: eV_0=\frac{hc}\lambda.
Photoelectric effect
hf=\phi+KE_{max}
  • The threshold frequency is f_0=\frac\phi h. Below it, no electrons are emitted, however intense the light.
  • A higher intensity means more photons per second, so more electrons, but not a higher KE_{max}.
  • Emission is instantaneous and one-to-one (one photon, one electron). This is evidence for the particle nature of light.
Wave–particle duality
\lambda=\frac hp=\frac h{mv}
  • Electron diffraction through graphite is evidence that particles behave as waves (spacing ≈ λ).
Worked example

UV of wavelength 200 nm falls on a metal with \phi=4.5 eV. E=\frac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.0\times10^8}{200\times10^{-9}}=9.9\times10^{-19}\text{ J}=6.2 eV, so KE_{max}=1.7 eV.

Exam tips

Convert between eV and J carefully. Wave theory can't explain the threshold frequency; only the photon model can.
p-5-1:
Temperature and phases
  • Thermal equilibrium: no net flow of energy between objects. T(\text{K})=\theta(^\circ\text{C})+273. Absolute zero (0 K) is the lowest possible internal energy.
  • Internal energy: the sum of the random kinetic and potential energies of the particles.
  • During a change of phase, T stays constant: the potential energy changes, not the kinetic energy.
Specific heat and latent heat
Q=mc\Delta\theta,\qquad Q=mL
  • c in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; L_f for fusion and L_v for vaporisation, in J kg⁻¹.
Ideal gases
pV=nRT=NkT
  • Assumptions: a large number of identical molecules moving randomly; negligible molecular volume; elastic collisions; no forces between molecules except during collisions; collision time much less than the time between collisions.
pV=\tfrac13Nm\overline{c^2},\qquad \tfrac12m\overline{c^2}=\tfrac32kT
  • k=\frac R{N_A}=1.38\times10^{-23}\text{ J K}^{-1}. The r.m.s. speed is \sqrt{\overline{c^2}}.
  • Boyle's law: pV is constant at constant T.
Worked example

Mean KE of a molecule at 300 K: \frac32\times1.38\times10^{-23}\times300=6.2\times10^{-21} J.

Exam tips

Always use kelvin in gas equations. n is in moles; N is the number of molecules.
p-5-2:
Circular motion
\omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}=2\pi f,\qquad v=\omega r
a=\frac{v^2}r=\omega^2r,\qquad F=\frac{mv^2}r=m\omega^2r
  • 1 radian is the angle subtended by an arc equal in length to the radius.
  • Constant speed but changing velocity, so it is accelerating towards the centre. The centripetal force is provided by something real (tension, gravity, friction, a reaction force).
Vertical circles
  • At the top: T+mg=\frac{mv^2}r. At the bottom: T-mg=\frac{mv^2}r.
  • Minimum speed at the top (string just slack): v=\sqrt{gr}.
Worked example

A 0.20 kg mass on a 0.50 m string moves at 3.0\text{ m s}^{-1} in a horizontal circle (on a table): F=\frac{0.20\times9.0}{0.50}=3.6 N.

Common mistakes
  • Using degrees in v=\omega r: angles must be in radians.
  • Saying an object in uniform circular motion is in equilibrium. Its velocity is changing, so there is a resultant force towards the centre.
  • At the top of a vertical circle the weight helps provide the centripetal force, so the tension is smallest there.
Exam tips

Centripetal force is not an extra force on the free-body diagram. It is the resultant of the real forces.
p-5-3:
SHM
a=-\omega^2x
  • SHM: the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and directed towards the equilibrium position.
x=A\cos\omega t
v=\pm\omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2},\qquad v_{max}=\omega A
  • The period is independent of amplitude (isochronous). Pendulum: T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac Lg}. Mass–spring: T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac mk}.
  • Energy swaps between KE and PE; the total is constant (\propto A^2) without damping.
Damping and resonance
  • Light damping: the amplitude decays gradually. Critical damping: returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating. Heavy damping: returns slowly.
  • Forced oscillations: resonance happens when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, giving maximum amplitude. Damping lowers and broadens the peak (and shifts it slightly lower).
Worked example

A=0.050 m, f=2.0 Hz: \omega=4\pi, so v_{max}=0.63\text{ m s}^{-1} and a_{max}=\omega^2A=7.9\text{ m s}^{-2}.

Exam tips

Use x=A\sin\omega t if timing starts at equilibrium, and \cos if it starts at maximum displacement. Set your calculator to radians.
p-5-4:
Fields
g=\frac Fm,\qquad g=-\frac{GM}{r^2}
  • Field lines are radial for a point mass and uniform close to the Earth's surface. G=6.67\times10^{-11}\text{ N m}^2\text{kg}^{-2}.
  • Newton's law: F=-\frac{GMm}{r^2}, which is attractive.
Orbits
  • Kepler 1: elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus. Kepler 2: equal areas in equal times. Kepler 3: T^2\propto r^3.
T^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3,\qquad v=\sqrt{\frac{GM}r}
  • Geostationary orbit: T=24 h, above the equator, moving in the same direction as the Earth spins.
Potential
V_g=-\frac{GM}r,\qquad E=-\frac{GMm}r
  • Potential is the work done per unit mass to bring a mass from infinity to that point. It is negative.
  • Escape velocity: v=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}r}.
  • The area under a force–distance graph is the work done (change in potential energy).
Exam tips

r is measured from the centre of the planet, so add the planet's radius to the height of the orbit.
p-5-5:
Stars
  • Life cycle: nebula, protostar, main sequence (H fusion). Low-mass stars become red giants, then white dwarfs. High-mass stars become red supergiants, then a supernova, leaving a neutron star or black hole.
  • Chandrasekhar limit: 1.44M_\odot; electron degeneracy pressure supports a white dwarf below it.
  • HR diagram: luminosity against temperature (temperature *decreasing* to the right).
Radiation
\lambda_{max}T=\text{constant}\ (2.9\times10^{-3}\text{ m K})
L=4\pi r^2\sigma T^4
  • Energy levels: \Delta E=hf. Emission and absorption line spectra. Grating: d\sin\theta=n\lambda.
Cosmology
  • Units: 1 AU (Earth–Sun distance), 1 ly, 1 pc ≈ 3.1\times10^{16} m. Parallax: p(\text{arcsec})=\frac1{d(\text{pc})}.
  • Doppler: \frac{\Delta\lambda}\lambda\approx\frac vc. Hubble's law v=H_0d; the age of the universe is about \frac1{H_0}.
  • Cosmological principle: the universe is isotropic and homogeneous on large scales. Evidence for the Big Bang: the CMB (about 2.7 K) and galactic redshift. Dark matter and dark energy.
Exam tips

Convert H_0 from km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ to s⁻¹ before computing the age: 1\text{ Mpc}=3.1\times10^{22} m.
p-6-1:
Key definitions
  • Capacitance: the charge stored per unit potential difference, C=\frac QV. Unit: the farad, 1\text{ F}=1\text{ C V}^{-1}. Typical values are µF (10⁻⁶) to nF (10⁻⁹).
  • A capacitor has two conducting plates separated by an insulator (the dielectric). Charge +Q builds on one plate and -Q on the other; no charge flows through the gap.
Combining capacitors
\text{parallel: } C=C_1+C_2+\dots\qquad\text{series: } \frac1C=\frac1{C_1}+\frac1{C_2}+\dots
  • These are the opposite of the resistor rules. In series each capacitor stores the same charge Q; in parallel each has the same p.d.
  • Parallel-plate capacitor: C=\frac{\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_rA}{d}, so a larger area or a smaller gap gives a larger capacitance.
Energy stored
W=\tfrac12QV=\tfrac12CV^2=\frac{Q^2}{2C}
  • The area under a V–Q graph (a straight line through the origin) is the energy stored.
  • When a battery charges a capacitor it does work QV, but only \frac12QV is stored; the other half is dissipated as heat in the resistance of the circuit.
Charging and discharging
\tau=RC
\text{discharge: } x=x_0e^{-t/RC}\quad(x = Q,\ V\text{ or }I)
\text{charging: } V=V_0\left(1-e^{-t/RC}\right)
Q=Q_0\left(1-e^{-t/RC}\right),\quad I=I_0e^{-t/RC}
  • After one time constant (t=RC) a discharging capacitor has e^{-1}=37\% of its starting value; a charging one has reached 63% of its final value.
  • Constant-ratio property: in equal time intervals the value falls by the same fraction, e.g. the time to halve is always t_{1/2}=RC\ln2\approx0.69RC.
  • Taking logs of the discharge equation: \ln V=\ln V_0-\frac{t}{RC}, so a graph of \ln V against t is a straight line with gradient -\frac1{RC}.
  • The area under an I–t graph is the charge that has flowed.
Modelling by iteration
  • Over a small time step \Delta t: \Delta Q=-\frac{Q}{RC}\Delta t. Repeating this in a spreadsheet gives the exponential decay; smaller \Delta t gives a more accurate model.
Worked examples

C=470\ \muF and R=10 kΩ give \tau=470\times10^{-6}\times10\times10^3=4.7 s. The time for the p.d. to halve is t=RC\ln2=3.3 s.

A 2200 µF capacitor is charged to 12 V. Energy stored: W=\frac12CV^2=\frac12\times2200\times10^{-6}\times144=0.16 J. Charge: Q=CV=0.026 C.

The p.d. across a discharging capacitor falls from 9.0 V to 3.0 V in 5.0 s. Then \frac{3}{9}=e^{-5/RC}, so RC=\frac{5.0}{\ln3}=4.6 s.

Uses
  • Flash guns and defibrillators (release stored energy quickly), back-up power for memory, smoothing a rectified supply, and timing circuits (choose RC).
Common mistakes
  • Forgetting to convert µF to F (×10⁻⁶) and kΩ to Ω (×10³).
  • Using the resistor rules for capacitors in series and parallel.
  • Thinking the current is constant: it is largest at the start and decays exponentially in both charging and discharging (it reverses direction on discharge).
Exam tips

If the question gives the time for the value to fall to a fraction, rearrange using natural logs: t=RC\ln\frac{x_0}{x}. Show the log step clearly for method marks.
p-6-2:
Key definitions
  • Electric field: a region in which a charged object experiences a force.
  • Electric field strength E: the force per unit positive charge, E=\frac Fq. Units: N C⁻¹ (equivalent to V m⁻¹). It is a vector, pointing in the direction of the force on a positive charge.
  • Field lines go from + to −; closer lines mean a stronger field.
Coulomb's law (point charges)
F=\frac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2},\qquad E=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}
  • Inverse-square law: doubling r quarters the force. A charged sphere behaves as if its charge were at its centre (for points outside it).
  • Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. \varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\text{ F m}^{-1} is the permittivity of free space.
Uniform fields
E=\frac Vd
  • Between parallel plates the field is uniform (equally spaced parallel lines), except near the edges.
  • A charged particle entering at right angles to a uniform field has a constant force F=qE perpendicular to its velocity, so it follows a parabola: constant velocity along the plates, constant acceleration a=\frac{qE}m across them.
  • Work done moving a charge through a p.d.: W=qV. An electron accelerated through V gains E_k=eV.
Electric potential
V=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r},\qquad E_p=qV=\frac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}
  • Electric potential at a point: the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small test charge from infinity to that point. It is zero at infinity, positive near a positive charge and negative near a negative charge.
  • Equipotentials are surfaces of constant potential; they are perpendicular to field lines, and no work is done moving along one.
  • Field strength is the potential gradient: E=-\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta r}. The area under an E–r graph is the change in potential.
  • Capacitance of an isolated sphere of radius R: C=4\pi\varepsilon_0R.
Comparison with gravitational fields
  • Both are inverse-square, both have \frac1r potentials, and both field strengths are force per unit (mass or charge).
  • Gravity acts on mass and is always attractive (so V_g is always negative). Electric forces act on charge and can attract or repel.
  • Electric forces between particles are vastly stronger: for two protons, the electric force is about 10^{36} times the gravitational force.
Worked examples

Force between charges of +2.0\ \muC and -3.0\ \muC, 0.10 m apart: F=\frac{2.0\times10^{-6}\times3.0\times10^{-6}}{4\pi\times8.85\times10^{-12}\times0.10^2}=5.4 N, attractive.

Plates 4.0 cm apart with a p.d. of 2000 V: E=\frac{2000}{0.040}=5.0\times10^4\text{ V m}^{-1}. Force on an electron: F=eE=1.60\times10^{-19}\times5.0\times10^4=8.0\times10^{-15} N.

Common mistakes
  • Forgetting to square r in Coulomb's law, or to convert cm to m and µC to C.
  • Using E=\frac Vd for a point charge: it applies only to a uniform field.
  • Mixing up E (field strength) with E_p (potential energy) and V (potential).
Exam tips

Keep signs on charges when calculating potential, but use magnitudes for the size of a force and state its direction (attract or repel) in words.
p-6-3:
Magnetic forces
F=BIL\sin\theta,\qquad F=BQv
  • Fleming's left-hand rule: First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current, thuMb = Motion.
  • 1 T is the field that exerts 1 N on 1 m of wire carrying 1 A perpendicular to the field.
  • A charged particle in a field moves in a circle: r=\frac{mv}{BQ}. Velocity selector: v=\frac EB.
Electromagnetic induction
\phi=BA\cos\theta,\qquad \varepsilon=-\frac{\Delta(N\phi)}{\Delta t}
  • Faraday: the induced e.m.f. equals the rate of change of flux linkage. Lenz: the induced current opposes the change that caused it.
  • Transformers: \frac{n_s}{n_p}=\frac{V_s}{V_p}=\frac{I_p}{I_s} (if 100% efficient).
Worked examples

A 0.050 m length of wire carries 3.0 A at right angles to a 0.20 T field: F=BIL=0.20\times3.0\times0.050=0.030 N.

A coil of 200 turns and area 4.0\times10^{-4} m² is in a 0.15 T field, which falls to zero in 0.020 s. Change of flux linkage =200\times0.15\times4.0\times10^{-4}=0.012 Wb-turns, so \varepsilon=\frac{0.012}{0.020}=0.60 V.

Common mistakes
  • Using the right hand for Fleming's motor rule. The left hand gives the force; the current direction is conventional current (opposite to electron flow).
  • Forgetting that a charged particle moving parallel to B feels no force (\sin0^\circ=0).
  • Confusing flux \phi (Wb) with flux density B (T).
Exam tips

Flux linkage N\phi has units Wb (or Wb-turns). Step-up transformers increase V and reduce I for transmission, giving smaller I^2R losses.
p-6-4:
The nucleus
  • Rutherford α-scattering: most pass straight through (atom mostly empty space); a few are deflected through large angles (small, dense, positive nucleus).
  • Radius R=r_0A^{1/3} with r_0\approx1.2 fm. Nuclear density is constant (about 10^{17}\text{ kg m}^{-3}).
  • Strong nuclear force: attractive up to about 3 fm, repulsive below about 0.5 fm.
Particles
  • Hadrons (baryons qqq, mesons q q̄) feel the strong force; leptons (e, μ, ν) do not.
  • Quarks: u +\frac23e, d -\frac13e, s -\frac13e. Proton uud, neutron udd.
  • β⁻ decay: d\to u+e^-+\bar\nu_e. β⁺ decay: u\to d+e^++\nu_e (weak interaction).
Radioactivity
A=\lambda N,\qquad N=N_0e^{-\lambda t},\qquad \lambda t_{1/2}=\ln2
  • α: 2p2n, highly ionising, stopped by paper. β: stopped by a few mm of aluminium. γ: reduced by lead.
Binding energy
\Delta E=\Delta mc^2
  • Mass defect: the mass of the separated nucleons minus the mass of the nucleus. Binding energy per nucleon peaks at Fe-56. Fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy ones both release energy.
  • 1 u =931.5 MeV.
Exam tips

Fission reactors: the moderator slows neutrons (elastic collisions), control rods absorb neutrons, and the coolant removes heat.
p-6-5:
X-rays
  • Produced when fast electrons hit a tungsten target (about 1% efficiency). Attenuation: I=I_0e^{-\mu x}.
  • Mechanisms: simple scatter (1–20 keV), photoelectric effect (< 100 keV), Compton scattering (0.5–5 MeV), pair production (> 1.02 MeV).
  • Contrast media (barium, iodine) have a high atomic number Z, so they absorb strongly. CAT scans build a 3D image from slices taken by a rotating X-ray tube.
Nuclear medicine
  • Tracers such as technetium-99m (γ emitter, 6 h half-life). Gamma camera: collimator, scintillator, photomultiplier tubes.
  • PET: a β⁺ tracer (e.g. F-18 in FDG). Annihilation produces two 511 keV γ photons in opposite directions.
Ultrasound
  • Above 20 kHz, produced with the piezoelectric effect. A-scan and B-scan. Doppler for blood flow: \Delta f=\frac{2fv\cos\theta}c.
  • Acoustic impedance Z=\rho c. Reflected fraction: \frac{I_r}{I_0}=\frac{(Z_2-Z_1)^2}{(Z_2+Z_1)^2}. Gel is used to match impedance, because air–skin reflects almost everything.
Exam tips

Compare techniques by resolution, ionising risk, cost and what they image (bone/soft tissue/function).
c-1-1:
Atomic structure
  • Proton: relative mass 1, charge +1. Neutron: mass 1, charge 0. Electron: mass 1/1836, charge −1.
  • Mass number A = protons + neutrons. Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so they share chemical properties.
Mass spectrometry (TOF)
  • Stages: ionisation (electron impact, X → X⁺ + e⁻; or electrospray, X + H⁺ → XH⁺), acceleration, ion drift, detection.
  • In electrospray the peak is at M_r+1.
KE=\tfrac12mv^2
t=d\sqrt{\frac{m}{2KE}}
A_r=\frac{\sum(\text{isotope mass}\times\text{abundance})}{\sum\text{abundance}}
Electron configuration
  • Order: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d. Exceptions: Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ and Cu is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹. When transition metals form ions, the 4s electrons are lost first.
Ionisation energy
  • First IE: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻. It depends on nuclear charge, distance from the nucleus, and shielding.
  • Down a group, IE decreases. Across a period it increases, with dips at Group 3 (the electron is in a p orbital) and Group 6 (pair repulsion).
  • Successive IEs show big jumps where a new shell is broken into, which gives the group.
Worked example

⁶⁹Ga 60.1%, ⁷¹Ga 39.9%: A_r=\frac{69\times60.1+71\times39.9}{100}=69.8.

Exam tips

Always include the state symbol (g) in IE equations.
c-1-2:
The mole
n=\frac{m}{M_r}
n=c\times V(\text{dm}^3)
pV=nRT
  • N_A=6.022\times10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}. For pV=nRT, use Pa, m³ and K (1 cm³ =10^{-6} m³).
Formulae and yields
  • Empirical formula: divide % by A_r, then by the smallest, then scale to whole numbers.
\%\text{ yield}=\frac{\text{actual}}{\text{theoretical}}\times100
\%\text{ AE}=\frac{M_r(\text{desired})}{\sum M_r(\text{products})}\times100
  • Water of crystallisation: heat to constant mass.
Titrations
  • Concordant titres agree within 0.10 cm³. Rinse the burette with the solution it will hold, and the pipette with the solution it will deliver.
Worked example

25.0 cm³ of NaOH needs 22.50 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄. Moles of acid =2.25\times10^{-3}, so NaOH =4.50\times10^{-3} mol (2 : 1), and [\text{NaOH}]=0.180\text{ mol dm}^{-3}.

Exam tips

Use the mole ratio from the balanced equation, and convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000.
c-1-3:
Bonding types
  • Ionic: electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice. High melting point; conducts when molten or dissolved.
  • Covalent: a shared pair of electrons. Dative: both electrons come from one atom (e.g. NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺).
  • Metallic: a lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.
  • Giant covalent: diamond (4 bonds, hard), graphite (3 bonds, delocalised electrons, conducts, layers slide), SiO₂.
Shapes (VSEPR)
  • Pairs: 2 linear 180°; 3 trigonal planar 120°; 4 tetrahedral 109.5°; 5 trigonal bipyramidal 90°/120°; 6 octahedral 90°.
  • Each lone pair reduces the angle by about 2.5°: NH₃ is 107° (pyramidal), H₂O is 104.5° (bent).
  • Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs.
Polarity and intermolecular forces
  • Electronegativity: the power of an atom to attract the pair of electrons in a covalent bond (F is highest).
  • Van der Waals (induced dipole) forces < permanent dipole–dipole forces < hydrogen bonds (N, O or F bonded to H, attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F).
  • Ice is less dense than water because hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice.
Exam tips

A symmetrical molecule with polar bonds (e.g. CO₂, CCl₄) is non-polar because the dipoles cancel.

  • When asked to explain a boiling point, name the force and say it is weak or strong relative to the others and needs more or less energy to overcome.
c-1-4:
Enthalpy
  • ΔH is the heat energy change at constant pressure. Exothermic: ΔH < 0. Standard conditions: 100 kPa and a stated temperature (usually 298 K).
  • \Delta_cH^\circ: 1 mol burned completely in oxygen. \Delta_fH^\circ: 1 mol formed from its elements in their standard states.
Calorimetry
q=mc\Delta T
\Delta H=-\frac{q}{n}
  • m is the mass of water or solution (not the fuel). c=4.18\text{ J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}.
Hess's law and bond enthalpies
  • The enthalpy change is independent of the route taken.
\Delta_rH=\sum\Delta_fH_{\text{prod}}-\sum\Delta_fH_{\text{react}}
\Delta_rH=\sum\Delta_cH_{\text{react}}-\sum\Delta_cH_{\text{prod}}
\Delta H=\sum(\text{bonds broken})-\sum(\text{bonds made})
  • Mean bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds, so results are less accurate.
Worked example

50.0 g of water rises by 12.0 K when 0.0100 mol of fuel burns: q=50.0\times4.18\times12.0=2508 J, so \Delta_cH=-251\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}.

Exam tips

Convert J to kJ and include the sign. Reasons a value is less exothermic than the data book: heat loss, incomplete combustion, non-standard conditions.
c-1-5:
Collision theory
  • To react, particles must collide with energy ≥ E_a and with the correct orientation.
  • Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution: the area under the curve is the total number of molecules. It starts at the origin and never touches the energy axis.
  • Higher T: the peak moves right and lower, and many more molecules have E\ge E_a. This is the main reason the rate rises.
  • Higher concentration or pressure: more frequent collisions.
  • Catalyst: provides an alternative route with a lower E_a, and is not used up.
Measuring rate
  • Rate = change in concentration per unit time. Use the gradient of a tangent.
  • Methods: gas volume (syringe), mass loss, colour change (colorimeter), clock reactions.
Exam tips

On M–B curves, the curve for a higher temperature has a lower peak, further to the right, with the same area.

  • Don't say "particles collide more" for temperature. Say "more particles have energy above E_a".
c-1-6:
Dynamic equilibrium
  • Forward and reverse rates are equal, and concentrations stay constant (closed system).
  • Le Chatelier: if a condition changes, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose the change.
  • Increasing pressure shifts to the side with fewer gas moles. Increasing T shifts in the endothermic direction. A catalyst doesn't change the position, only how fast equilibrium is reached.
Kc

For a\text{A}+b\text{B}\rightleftharpoons c\text{C}+d\text{D}:

K_c=\frac{[\text{C}]^c[\text{D}]^d}{[\text{A}]^a[\text{B}]^b}
  • Only temperature changes K_c. Units: cancel the concentration terms.
  • Use an ICE table (initial, change, equilibrium). Divide moles by volume to get concentrations.
Industrial compromises
  • Haber process: 450 °C (rate vs yield), 200 atm (yield vs cost and safety), iron catalyst.
Worked example

H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI. Start with 1.0 mol of each in 1.0 dm³; 0.80 mol HI at equilibrium, so 0.60 mol each of H₂ and I₂ remain. K_c=\frac{0.80^2}{0.60^2}=1.78 (no units).

Exam tips

If the forward reaction is exothermic, increasing T decreases K_c.
c-1-7:
Redox
  • OIL RIG: oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain. An oxidising agent is reduced itself.
  • Oxidation state rules: elements 0; O is −2 (−1 in peroxides); H is +1 (−1 in metal hydrides); F is −1; the sum equals the overall charge.
Half-equations (acidic)

1. Balance the atoms other than O and H.

2. Add H₂O to balance O.

3. Add H⁺ to balance H.

4. Add e⁻ to balance the charge.

  • E.g. MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O.
  • To combine, multiply so the electrons cancel.
Exam tips

Name the oxidising agent as the species, e.g. "MnO₄⁻ ions", not just "Mn".

  • Disproportionation: the same element is both oxidised and reduced (e.g. Cl₂ in water).
c-1-8:
Born–Haber cycles
  • Lattice enthalpy of formation: gaseous ions → 1 mol of solid lattice (exothermic). AQA also uses lattice dissociation, which is endothermic.
  • Steps: atomisation, ionisation energy(s), electron affinity(s), lattice enthalpy, and \Delta_fH.
  • The second electron affinity of O is endothermic (adding an electron to a negative ion).
  • A more negative (exothermic) lattice formation enthalpy comes from smaller, more highly charged ions.
  • Perfect ionic model vs experimental: a difference means covalent character (polarisation).
Solutions
\Delta_{sol}H=\Delta_{LE,diss}H+\sum\Delta_{hyd}H
Entropy and Gibbs
  • Entropy S is disorder: gas > liquid > solid. More moles of gas means \Delta S>0.
\Delta S=\sum S_{products}-\sum S_{reactants}
\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S
  • Feasible if \Delta G\le0. At the changeover T=\frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}. Convert \Delta S from J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ to kJ.
Worked example

\Delta H=+178 kJ mol⁻¹ and \Delta S=+161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (CaCO₃ decomposition): T=\frac{178}{0.161}=1106 K.

Exam tips

Feasible doesn't mean fast: a large E_a can make a feasible reaction negligibly slow.
c-1-9:
Rate equations
\text{rate}=k[\text{A}]^m[\text{B}]^n
  • Orders are found by experiment, not from the equation. The overall order is m+n.
  • Order 0: rate is independent of concentration. Order 1: rate ∝ concentration. Order 2: doubling the concentration gives 4× the rate.
  • Concentration–time graphs: order 0 is a straight line; order 1 has a constant half-life. Rate–concentration graphs: order 0 is horizontal, order 1 is a straight line through the origin, order 2 is a curve.
  • Units of k come from rearranging, e.g. for a 2nd-order reaction: mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹.
Arrhenius
k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}
\ln k=\ln A-\frac{E_a}{R}\cdot\frac1T
  • A plot of \ln k against \frac1T has gradient -\frac{E_a}R.
Rate-determining step
  • The slowest step. Species in the rate equation appear in (or before) the RDS.
Worked example

A gradient of -6000 K gives E_a=6000\times8.31=49.9\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}.

Exam tips

Initial rates come from the tangent at t=0. A clock reaction gives rate ∝ \frac1t.
c-1-10:
Kp
  • Partial pressure p_A=x_AP, where the mole fraction is x_A=\frac{n_A}{n_{total}}.

For a\text{A}(g)\rightleftharpoons b\text{B}(g):

K_p=\frac{(p_B)^b}{(p_A)^a}
  • Only gases appear in K_p (in heterogeneous equilibria, leave out the solids).
  • Only temperature changes K_p. Changing the pressure moves the position, but K_p stays the same.
Worked example

N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ at 100 kPa, with mole fractions 0.6 and 0.4: p_{NO_2}=40 and p_{N_2O_4}=60, so K_p=\frac{40^2}{60}=26.7 kPa.

Worked example 2 (from moles)

2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ at a total pressure of 200 kPa. At equilibrium there are 0.20 mol SO₂, 0.10 mol O₂ and 1.70 mol SO₃ (2.00 mol in total).

  • Mole fractions are 0.10, 0.05 and 0.85, so the partial pressures are 20, 10 and 170 kPa.
K_p=\frac{170^2}{20^2\times10}=7.2\text{ kPa}^{-1}
Effect of conditions
  • If the forward reaction is exothermic, raising T makes K_p smaller, so the yield falls.
  • Adding an inert gas at constant volume does not change the partial pressures, so the position does not move.
Exam tips

Check that the mole fractions sum to 1 and give the units of K_p (kPa raised to some power, or none).
c-1-11:
Electrode potentials
  • Standard hydrogen electrode: H₂ at 100 kPa, 1.00 mol dm⁻³ H⁺, Pt, 298 K. E° = 0.00 V.
  • Cell notation: oxidised species next to the salt bridge, e.g. Zn ∣ Zn²⁺ ∥ Cu²⁺ ∣ Cu.
E_{cell}^\circ=E_{right}^\circ-E_{left}^\circ=E_{red}^\circ-E_{ox}^\circ
  • The more positive E° couple is reduced (it is the stronger oxidising agent). The reaction is feasible if E_{cell}>0.
  • Salt bridge: filter paper soaked in KNO₃(aq), which lets ions move.
Cells
  • Non-rechargeable: e.g. alkaline cells. Rechargeable: lithium-ion; the reactions reverse on charging.
  • Fuel cell: H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O. In alkali: anode H₂ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O + 2e⁻; cathode O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. E ≈ 1.23 V. The only product is water, but H₂ needs energy to produce.
Worked example

Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V and Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V: E_{cell}=0.80-(-0.76)=1.56 V. Overall: Zn + 2Ag⁺ → Zn²⁺ + 2Ag.

Exam tips

Do not multiply E° values when you balance electrons.
c-1-12:
Definitions
  • Brønsted–Lowry acid: proton donor. Base: proton acceptor.
\text{pH}=-\log_{10}[\text{H}^+]
K_w=[\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-]=1.0\times10^{-14}\ (298\text{ K})
  • Pure water is always neutral: [H⁺] = [OH⁻], even when the pH is not 7 (e.g. at higher T).
Weak acids
K_a=\frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]}
[\text{H}^+]\approx\sqrt{K_ac}
pK_a=-\log K_a
  • At half-neutralisation, pH = pK_a.
Buffers
  • A buffer resists pH change when small amounts of acid or base are added. Acidic buffer: a weak acid plus its salt (e.g. CH₃COOH / CH₃COONa).
[\text{H}^+]=K_a\frac{[\text{HA}]}{[\text{A}^-]}
  • Blood is buffered by H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻.
Titration curves
  • Indicators: methyl orange (pH 3–4.5) for strong acid–weak base; phenolphthalein (pH 8–10) for weak acid–strong base. There is no sharp end-point for weak–weak titrations.
Worked example

0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid with K_a=1.74\times10^{-5}: [\text{H}^+]=1.32\times10^{-3}, so pH = 2.88.

Exam tips

For a strong base, find [OH⁻] first, then [\text{H}^+]=\frac{K_w}{[\text{OH}^-]}. For a diprotic strong acid, [\text{H}^+]=2c.
c-2-1:
Periodicity
  • Elements are arranged by proton number into s, p, d and f blocks. Period 3: Na and Mg are s-block; Al to Ar are p-block.
  • Atomic radius decreases across a period: nuclear charge increases while shielding stays similar.
  • First IE increases across a period, with dips at Al (3p electron, higher energy, more shielded) and S (pair repulsion in a 3p orbital).
Melting points across Period 3
  • Na < Mg < Al: metallic bonding gets stronger (more delocalised electrons, smaller ions with higher charge).
  • Si is highest: giant covalent, so many strong covalent bonds must break.
  • P₄, S₈, Cl₂, Ar: simple molecular, with weak van der Waals forces. S₈ > P₄ > Cl₂ > Ar because bigger molecules have more electrons.
Exam tips

Explain trends using charge, distance and shielding for IE and radius, and the type and strength of bonding for melting points.
c-2-2:
Group 2 trends (down the group)
  • Atomic radius increases, first IE decreases, and reactivity increases.
  • Melting point generally decreases (larger ions, weaker metallic bonding).
  • Hydroxide solubility increases (Mg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble). Sulfate solubility decreases (BaSO₄ is insoluble).
Reactions
  • With water: M + 2H₂O → M(OH)₂ + H₂. Mg reacts very slowly with cold water but burns in steam: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂.
  • Test for sulfate: acidified BaCl₂ gives a white BaSO₄ precipitate. HCl is added first to remove carbonate.
Uses
  • Mg(OH)₂: antacid. Ca(OH)₂: neutralising acidic soil. BaSO₄: barium meal (it's insoluble, so not toxic).
  • CaO or CaCO₃: removing SO₂ from flue gases. Mg: extracting Ti from TiCl₄ (TiCl₄ + 2Mg → Ti + 2MgCl₂).
Exam tips

Barium compounds are toxic, but BaSO₄ is safe because it is insoluble. Say that explicitly.
c-2-3:
Halogen trends
  • Down the group: boiling point increases (more van der Waals), electronegativity decreases, and oxidising ability decreases.
  • Appearance: F₂ pale yellow gas; Cl₂ pale green gas; Br₂ red-brown liquid; I₂ grey-black solid (purple vapour).
  • Displacement: a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide. Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂ (orange).
Halide ions as reducing agents
  • Reducing power increases down the group (larger ions lose an electron more easily).
  • With concentrated H₂SO₄: NaCl gives HCl only. NaBr gives HBr, Br₂ and SO₂. NaI gives HI, I₂, SO₂, S and H₂S (bad-egg smell).
Silver halide test
  • Add dilute HNO₃ (to remove CO₃²⁻ and OH⁻), then AgNO₃(aq). AgCl is white and dissolves in dilute NH₃. AgBr is cream and dissolves in concentrated NH₃. AgI is yellow and is insoluble in NH₃.
Chlorine
  • Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO is disproportionation; it is used to treat water (kills bacteria). In sunlight: 2Cl₂ + 2H₂O → 4HCl + O₂.
  • Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O makes bleach (cold, dilute alkali).
Exam tips

Explain the risk–benefit of chlorinating water: it's toxic, and can form chlorinated hydrocarbons, but it prevents disease.
c-2-4:
Reactions with oxygen
  • Na → Na₂O (yellow flame); Mg → MgO (white flame); Al → Al₂O₃; Si → SiO₂; P → P₄O₁₀ (white flame); S → SO₂ (blue flame).
Oxides
  • Na₂O, MgO and Al₂O₃ are giant ionic, with high melting points. SiO₂ is giant covalent, with a very high melting point. P₄O₁₀ and SO₂ are simple molecular, with low melting points.
  • With water: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH (pH 12–14). MgO gives pH about 9. Al₂O₃ and SiO₂ are insoluble. P₄O₁₀ + 6H₂O → 4H₃PO₄ (pH 0–1). SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄.
Acid–base behaviour
  • Basic oxides: Na₂O and MgO react with acids. Amphoteric: Al₂O₃ reacts with both acids and alkalis (Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2NaAl(OH)₄).
  • Acidic oxides: SiO₂ (with hot concentrated NaOH, forming Na₂SiO₃), P₄O₁₀ (forming Na₃PO₄), SO₂ and SO₃.
Exam tips

Link the structure of each oxide to its melting point and its reaction with water, in the same answer.
c-2-5:
What a transition metal is
  • It forms at least one stable ion with a partially filled d sub-shell. Properties: complexes, coloured ions, variable oxidation states, catalysis.
Complexes
  • Ligand: donates a lone pair to form a coordinate (dative) bond. Monodentate: H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻. Bidentate: en, C₂O₄²⁻. Multidentate: EDTA⁴⁻ (hexadentate).
  • Shapes: octahedral (6 small ligands), tetrahedral (4 Cl⁻, e.g. [CuCl₄]²⁻), square planar (cisplatin), linear ([Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺).
  • Isomerism: cis/trans (octahedral and square planar); optical (with 3 bidentate ligands).
  • Chelate effect: multidentate ligands substitute monodentate ones because the number of particles increases, so ΔS > 0.
  • Haem contains Fe²⁺. CO binds more strongly than O₂, which is why CO is toxic.
Colour
\Delta E=hf=\frac{hc}\lambda
  • The d orbitals split. Electrons absorb visible light and are promoted; the complementary colour is seen. Colour depends on the metal, its oxidation state, the ligands and the coordination number.
  • Colorimetry: measure absorbance against concentration with a calibration curve.
Redox titrations and catalysis
  • MnO₄⁻ (self-indicating, colourless → pale pink). MnO₄⁻ : Fe²⁺ = 1 : 5. Cr₂O₇²⁻ : Fe²⁺ = 1 : 6.
  • Heterogeneous catalysis: V₂O₅ (Contact process), Fe (Haber). Homogeneous: Fe²⁺ for S₂O₈²⁻ + I⁻. Autocatalysis: Mn²⁺ in MnO₄⁻/C₂O₄²⁻.
Exam tips

Zn and Sc are d-block but not transition metals: Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰ and Sc³⁺ is d⁰.
c-2-6:
Metal-aqua ions
  • [M(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is weakly acidic. [M(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is more acidic because of its higher charge density, which polarises O–H more:
  • [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ + H₂O ⇌ [Fe(H₂O)₅(OH)]²⁺ + H₃O⁺.
Precipitates
  • Cu²⁺: blue solution; blue Cu(H₂O)₄(OH)₂ precipitate. In excess NH₃ it forms deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺.
  • Fe²⁺: green precipitate, which goes brown in air. Fe³⁺: orange-brown precipitate.
  • Al³⁺: white precipitate, which dissolves in excess NaOH to give [Al(OH)₄(H₂O)₂]⁻ (amphoteric).
  • With Na₂CO₃: 2+ ions give MCO₃ precipitates; 3+ ions give M(OH)₃ precipitates plus CO₂ bubbles.
Ligand substitution
  • [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CuCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O (blue → yellow-green; octahedral → tetrahedral).
Worked example

A solution of [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ has a lower pH than one of [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ of the same concentration. The 3+ ion has a higher charge density, so it polarises the O–H bonds in the water ligands more, releasing H⁺ more readily.

Common mistakes
  • Writing that NH₃ dissolves all hydroxide precipitates: of the ions in this topic, excess NH₃ dissolves only the copper hydroxide precipitate (forming [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺).
  • Forgetting the CO₂ bubbles when 3+ ions react with carbonate.
Exam tips

Learn the colours as tables (ion × reagent × few drops/excess). They are easy marks.
c-3-1:
Nomenclature and formulae
  • Formula types: molecular, empirical, structural, displayed, skeletal. General formulae: alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, alkenes CₙH₂ₙ.
  • Naming: find the longest chain, number from the end giving the lowest locants, and list substituents alphabetically (2-chloro-3-methylbutane).
Isomerism
  • Structural isomers: chain, position and functional-group isomers (e.g. propanal and propanone).
  • Stereoisomers: E/Z isomerism needs restricted rotation about C=C and two different groups on each carbon.
  • CIP rules: the atom with the higher atomic number has priority. Z means the priority groups are on the same side; E means opposite sides.
Reaction types
  • Homolytic fission gives radicals. Heterolytic fission gives ions.
  • Curly arrows show the movement of an electron pair, from a bond or lone pair to an atom or bond.
Exam tips

Use skeletal formulae carefully: every corner and end of a line is a carbon, and H atoms on carbon are not shown.
c-3-2:
Alkanes and fuels
  • Saturated hydrocarbons. Fractional distillation of crude oil: there is a temperature gradient in the column; smaller molecules condense higher up.
  • Thermal cracking: high T and pressure, making many alkenes. Catalytic cracking: zeolite, about 450 °C, slight pressure, making aromatics and branched alkanes.
Combustion and pollution
  • Complete: CO₂ + H₂O. Incomplete: CO (toxic) and C (soot).
  • NOₓ forms from N₂ + O₂ at high engine temperatures. SO₂ forms from sulfur impurities and causes acid rain; it is removed with CaO.
  • Catalytic converter (Pt/Rh): 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂.
Free-radical substitution
  • Initiation: Cl₂ → 2Cl• (UV).
  • Propagation: CH₄ + Cl• → •CH₃ + HCl, then •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•.
  • Termination: two radicals combine, e.g. •CH₃ + •CH₃ → C₂H₆.
  • Ozone depletion: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂, then ClO• + O₃ → 2O₂ + Cl•. Cl• is regenerated, so it acts as a catalyst.
Exam tips

Further substitution gives a mixture of products, so free-radical substitution is a poor way to make one specific product.
c-3-3:
Halogenoalkanes
  • C–X is polar (C is δ+). Reactivity depends on bond enthalpy: C–I is the weakest, so it is hydrolysed fastest.
Nucleophilic substitution
  • OH⁻ (warm NaOH(aq), reflux) gives an alcohol. CN⁻ (KCN in ethanol/water) gives a nitrile, adding one carbon. NH₃ (excess, in ethanol, under pressure) gives a primary amine.
  • Mechanism: the nucleophile's lone pair attacks the δ+ C, and the C–X bond breaks heterolytically, releasing X⁻.
Elimination
  • KOH in ethanol, hot: OH⁻ acts as a base, removes H⁺ from the adjacent carbon, forms C=C, and X⁻ leaves.
  • Tertiary halogenoalkanes favour elimination; primary ones favour substitution.
Rate experiment
  • Water + AgNO₃ in ethanol at the same temperature: time how long the precipitate takes to form (I fastest, then Br, then Cl).
Exam tips

In mechanisms, draw the lone pair on the nucleophile and the δ+/δ− dipole on C–X. Arrows start at the lone pair or bond.
c-3-4:
Alkenes
  • C=C is a σ bond plus a π bond. The π electrons are a region of high electron density, so alkenes attract electrophiles.
  • Bromine water changes from orange to colourless.
Electrophilic addition
  • HBr gives a bromoalkane. Br₂ gives a dibromoalkane (Br₂ is polarised by the C=C). Cold concentrated H₂SO₄ gives an alkyl hydrogensulfate, which then forms an alcohol with water.
  • Mechanism: π electrons attack the electrophile, forming a carbocation intermediate; then Br⁻ attacks.
  • Markovnikov: the major product comes from the more stable carbocation (tertiary > secondary > primary). Alkyl groups have a positive inductive effect.
Addition polymers
  • Poly(ethene), poly(propene) and PVC are made from alkenes. Repeat unit: –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–.
  • They are unreactive (strong non-polar C–C and C–H bonds), so they are not biodegradable. Plasticisers make PVC flexible.
Exam tips

For an unsymmetrical alkene, draw the carbocation and say why it is the more stable one.
c-3-5:
Making ethanol
  • Hydration of ethene: steam, H₃PO₄ catalyst, 300 °C, 60–70 atm. Fast and pure, but uses finite crude oil.
  • Fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, with yeast at 35 °C and no oxygen. Renewable, but slow, and the product needs distilling.
  • Bioethanol is called carbon-neutral, though in practice farming and transport release CO₂.
Oxidation (acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, orange → green)
  • Primary: aldehyde (distil it off as it forms), then carboxylic acid (reflux, excess oxidant).
  • Secondary: ketone. Tertiary: not oxidised.
  • Tests: Tollens' gives a silver mirror and Fehling's gives a brick-red precipitate with aldehydes, but not with ketones.
Elimination
  • Dehydration with concentrated H₃PO₄ or H₂SO₄ gives an alkene and water. This makes alkenes from renewable sources.
Exam tips

Use [O] in oxidation equations: CH₃CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CHO + H₂O.
c-3-6:
Tests for functional groups
  • Alkene: bromine water decolourised. Aldehyde: Tollens' or Fehling's. Carboxylic acid: NaHCO₃ fizzes (CO₂).
  • Primary or secondary alcohol: acidified dichromate turns green. Halogenoalkane: NaOH(aq), then HNO₃, then AgNO₃.
Mass spectrometry
  • The M⁺ peak gives M_r. High-resolution MS (to 4 d.p.) distinguishes compounds with the same integer M_r.
Infrared spectroscopy
  • Bonds absorb IR at characteristic wavenumbers: O–H (alcohol) 3230–3550 broad; O–H (acid) 2500–3000 very broad; C=O 1680–1750; C–H 2850–3300.
  • Fingerprint region: below 1500 cm⁻¹, used to match a compound to a known spectrum.
  • Greenhouse gases (CO₂, H₂O, CH₄) absorb IR, which contributes to global warming.
Exam tips

Quote the bond and the range from the data sheet when you identify an IR peak.
c-3-7:
Key definitions
  • Stereoisomers: same structural formula but a different arrangement of atoms in space. Optical isomerism is one type (E/Z is the other).
  • Chiral centre (asymmetric carbon): a carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups. Mark it with an asterisk, C*.
  • Enantiomers (optical isomers): a pair of molecules that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.
  • Racemic mixture (racemate): an equimolar (50 : 50) mixture of two enantiomers.
Plane-polarised light
  • Each enantiomer rotates the plane of plane-polarised light by the same angle but in opposite directions.
  • A racemic mixture is optically inactive: the two rotations cancel out.
  • Enantiomers have identical physical properties (melting point, boiling point, density) and identical chemical reactions, except with other chiral molecules (e.g. enzymes and receptors in the body).
Spotting chiral centres
  • Check each sp³ carbon. A carbon with two H atoms (CH₂), or two identical groups such as two CH₃ groups, cannot be chiral.
  • A C=C or C=O carbon is never a chiral centre (only three groups, planar).
  • Look along the whole chain: in butan-2-ol, C2 carries H, OH, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃, which are all different, so it is chiral. Propan-2-ol (two CH₃ groups) is not.
Forming racemic mixtures
  • The C=O group is planar. In nucleophilic addition (e.g. KCN then acid with ethanal), CN⁻ can attack from either face with equal probability, giving equal amounts of both enantiomers.
  • The same happens in electrophilic addition when a planar carbocation is attacked to make a new chiral centre, e.g. HBr + but-1-ene → racemic 2-bromobutane.
  • A reaction that makes only one enantiomer (e.g. an enzyme-catalysed reaction) gives an optically active product.
Worked example

Is 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid), CH₃CH(OH)COOH, chiral?

C2 is bonded to H, OH, CH₃ and COOH: four different groups, so C2 is a chiral centre and the molecule has two enantiomers. C1 (COOH) and C3 (CH₃) are not chiral.

Draw the pair as a 3D tetrahedral C with one wedge and one dash bond, then reflect it in a mirror line, so that two groups swap sides.

Drugs and synthesis
  • Often only one enantiomer of a drug binds to the target receptor. The other may be inactive or harmful (the thalidomide tragedy).
  • Synthetic routes through planar intermediates give racemates, which then need costly separation; chemists use chiral catalysts or enzymes to make a single enantiomer.
Common mistakes
  • Saying enantiomers have different boiling points or react differently with ordinary reagents: they do not.
  • Drawing the "mirror image" as the same molecule rotated. Swap two groups or reflect it properly.
  • Forgetting that a racemic mixture has no effect on plane-polarised light.
Exam tips

For "explain why the product is optically inactive", give three points: the C=O (or carbocation) is planar; attack is equally likely from above and below; a racemic mixture forms, whose rotations cancel.
c-3-8:
Aldehydes and ketones
  • Both contain C=O. Aldehydes: RCHO. Ketones: RCOR'.
  • Aldehydes are oxidised (Tollens' gives a silver mirror; Fehling's turns from blue to a brick-red Cu₂O precipitate). Ketones are not.
Nucleophilic addition
  • NaBH₄ (reduction, [H]): aldehyde → primary alcohol; ketone → secondary alcohol. The nucleophile is H⁻.
